body_md:
\label{thrm:main}
Under Setting~\ref{TheSetting}, let $D=2^{46d}$ and choose $\mu\in\Delta_{N:D}$ 
\footnote{Note that such a $\mu$ must exist by Lemma~\ref{lem:three-doubling-weights}.}.     
  
Then the calibrated reconstruction $F=F_1$ defined by~\eqref{eq:entropy-variance-extension__primal___SITES}--\eqref{eq:entropy-variance-extension__specialization} is definable in $\mathbb{R}_{\operatorname{exp}}$ and satisfies:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] \textbf{Interpolation:} For every $n\in [N]$ and $j\in\{0,\dots,s\}$ we have
\[
    D^jF(X_n)
=
    D^jP_n(X_n)
.
\]
\item[(ii)] \textbf{Regularity:} $F\in\dot{C}^{s,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ and there is a constant\footnote{Depending only on $d,s$.} $K_{d,s}\ge1$ satisfying
\[
    [F]_{s,1}\le K_{d,s}M,
\]
Moreover, $K_{d,s}
    \in
    \mathcal{O}
    (
        \mathrm{e}^{cd}(d+s)^{cs}
    )$ for some absolute $c>0$ and 
$K_{d,s}=1$ when $s<2$.
   
\item[(iv)] \textbf{Extrapolation:} If, moreover, $s\ge 2$ then, $F$ is real-analytic on $\mathbb{R}^d\setminus\{X_n\}_{n=1}^N$.
\end{enumerate}

\label{dataformat}
Fix $d,s\in\mathbb N_+$. The word inputs are $N\in\mathbb N_+$ and an integer $q\ge2s+2$. The exact-real inputs are $M>0$ and $(X_i,\mu_i,(c_{i,\alpha})_{\alpha\in\Lambda_{d,s}})_{i\in[N]}$, where the sites $X_i\in\mathbb R^d$ are pairwise distinct and $\mu=(\mu_i)_{i\in[N]}\in\Delta_N^\circ$. Each polynomial $P_i\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_d]$, of degree at most $s$, is represented by its centered coefficients:
\[
P_i(x)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{\alpha\in\Lambda_{d,s}}c_{i,\alpha}(x-X_i)^\alpha,\qquad i\in[N].
\]

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\mathbb B(z,\rho)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{y\in\mathbb R^d:|y-z|<\rho\}$, $v_d\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mathcal L^d(\mathbb B(0,1))>0$, $T_e\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\varphi^{-1}(\{e\})$, $n_e\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}|T_e|$, and $w_t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\nu_{\varphi(t)}$. For $e\in S$, surjectivity and separation give
\[
\begin{gathered}
1\le n_e,\qquad \mathbb B(t,r/(2A))\cap\mathbb B(t',r/(2A))=\varnothing\quad(t,t'\in T_e,\ t\ne t'),\\
\bigcup_{t\in T_e}\mathbb B(t,r/(2A))\subseteq\mathbb B(e,r+r/(2A)),\\
n_ev_d(r/(2A))^d\le v_d(r+r/(2A))^d,\qquad n_e\le(2A+1)^d<A^{2d}=B.
\end{gathered}
\]
For $a,b\in T$, \eqref{eq:three-parent-weight-comparison} yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
|a-b|<8r/A&\Longrightarrow |\varphi(a)-\varphi(b)|\le|\varphi(a)-a|+|a-b|+|b-\varphi(b)|\\
&\hspace{37mm}<(2+8/A)r<4r\Longrightarrow w_a\le B^2w_b.
\end{aligned}
\]

Enumerate $\mathcal E\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{\{a,b\}:a,b\in T,\ a\ne b,\ |a-b|<4r/A\}=\{E_1,\ldots,E_L\}$ without repetition, allowing $L=0$, and put $u_t^0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} w_t/n_{\varphi(t)}$. Recursively, for $1\le k\le L$ and $E_k=\{a,b\}$, set $u^k=u^{k-1}$ if $\max(u_a^{k-1},u_b^{k-1})\le B^2\min(u_a^{k-1},u_b^{k-1})$. Otherwise, let $(g_k,h_k)$ be the ordering of $E_k$ satisfying $u_{g_k}^{k-1}>B^2u_{h_k}^{k-1}$ and set
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-pair-weight-update}
\begin{aligned}
\delta_k&\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{u_{g_k}^{k-1}-B^2u_{h_k}^{k-1}}{B^2+1},&u_t^k&\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} u_t^{k-1}+\delta_k\bigl(\mathbf1_{\{t=h_k\}}-\mathbf1_{\{t=g_k\}}\bigr),\\
u_{g_k}^k&=\frac{B^2(u_{g_k}^{k-1}+u_{h_k}^{k-1})}{B^2+1},&u_{h_k}^k&=\frac{u_{g_k}^{k-1}+u_{h_k}^{k-1}}{B^2+1}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Let $\mathcal I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,L\}$ consist of the nonidentity updates. We prove by induction that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-transfer-intervals}
0<w_t/B\le u_t^k\le w_t\quad(t\in T),\qquad \sum_{t\in T}u_t^k=1\qquad(0\le k\le L).
\end{equation}
At $k=0$, $1\le n_e<B$ and $\sum_{t\in T}u_t^0=\sum_{e\in S}n_e\nu_e/n_e=1$. For $k\in\mathcal I$, abbreviate $g=g_k$, $h=h_k$. The inductive hypothesis and \eqref{eq:three-pair-weight-update} imply $0<\delta_k<u_g^{k-1}$, $u_g^k=B^2u_h^k$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
w_g/B&\le Bw_h\le B^2u_h^{k-1}\le B^2u_h^k=u_g^k\le u_g^{k-1}\le w_g,\\
w_h/B&\le u_h^{k-1}\le u_h^k=u_g^k/B^2\le u_g^{k-1}/B^2\le w_g/B^2\le w_h,\\
\sum_{t\in T}u_t^k&=\sum_{t\in T}u_t^{k-1}+\delta_k(1-1)=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The remaining coordinates and the steps $k\notin\mathcal I$ are unchanged.

Put $\mathcal Q_k\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{\{a,b\}\in\mathcal E:\max(u_a^k,u_b^k)\le B^2\min(u_a^k,u_b^k)\}$. Fix $k\in\mathcal I$, $g=g_k$, $h=h_k$, and $t\in T\setminus\{g,h\}$. For $\{g,t\}\in\mathcal Q_{k-1}$, $|t-h|\le|t-g|+|g-h|<8r/A$, so
\[
u_g^k\le u_g^{k-1}\le B^2u_t^{k-1}=B^2u_t^k,\qquad u_t^k\le w_t\le B^2w_h\le Bu_g^k\le B^2u_g^k.
\]
For $\{h,t\}\in\mathcal Q_{k-1}$, $|g-t|\le|g-h|+|h-t|<8r/A$, so
\[
u_t^k=u_t^{k-1}\le B^2u_h^{k-1}\le B^2u_h^k,\qquad u_h^k=u_g^k/B^2\le w_g/B^2\le w_t\le Bu_t^k\le B^2u_t^k.
\]
Moreover, $u_g^k=B^2u_h^k$ and $E\cap\{g,h\}=\varnothing$ implies $(u_t^k)_{t\in E}=(u_t^{k-1})_{t\in E}$. Consequently,
\[
k\notin\mathcal I\ \Longrightarrow\ \mathcal Q_k=\mathcal Q_{k-1}\ni E_k,\qquad \mathcal Q_k\supseteq\mathcal Q_{k-1}\cup\{E_k\}\quad(1\le k\le L),\qquad \mathcal Q_L\supseteq\bigcup_{k=1}^L\{E_k\}=\mathcal E.
\]
Set $\nu'_t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} u_t^L$. Then $\mathcal Q_L=\mathcal E$, $B\ge256>1$, and~\eqref{eq:three-transfer-intervals} give
\[
\sum_{t\in T}\nu'_t=1,\qquad 0<B^{-1}\nu_{\varphi(t)}\le\nu'_t\le\nu_{\varphi(t)},\qquad \nu'_t\le B^2\nu'_{t'}\quad(|t-t'|<4r/A),
\]
where $t=t'$ uses $B^2\ge1$.

Define $a_{gh}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{k\in\mathcal I:(g_k,h_k)=(g,h)}\delta_k$ for $g,h\in T$ and $\mathcal D\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{(g,h)\in T^2:a_{gh}>0\}$. For every $k\in\mathcal I$, \eqref{eq:three-transfer-intervals} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-transfer-parent-decrease}
w_{g_k}\ge u_{g_k}^{k-1}>B^2u_{h_k}^{k-1}\ge Bw_{h_k}.
\end{equation}
If $(g,h),(h,t)\in\mathcal D$, then $|g-t|\le|g-h|+|h-t|<8r/A$ and $w_g>Bw_h>B^2w_t$, contradicting $w_g\le B^2w_t$. Hence
\[
a_{gh}a_{ht}=0\quad(g,h,t\in T),\qquad O_t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{h\in T}a_{th},\quad I_t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{g\in T}a_{gt},\quad O_tI_t=\sum_{g,h\in T}a_{gt}a_{th}=0.
\]
Summing \eqref{eq:three-pair-weight-update} over $k$ gives $u_t^L=u_t^0-O_t+I_t$. In particular,
\[
c_t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} u_t^0-O_t=\begin{cases}u_t^0,&O_t=0,\\u_t^L,&O_t>0,\end{cases}\qquad c_t>0,\qquad \pi_{e,t}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mathbf1_{\{e=\varphi(t)\}}c_t+\sum_{g\in T:\varphi(g)=e}a_{gt}\ge0.
\]
For $e\in S$ and $t\in T$,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{t\in T}\pi_{e,t}&=\sum_{t\in T_e}(u_t^0-O_t)+\sum_{g\in T_e}\sum_{t\in T}a_{gt}=\sum_{t\in T_e}u_t^0=\nu_e,\\
\sum_{e\in S}\pi_{e,t}&=c_t+\sum_{g\in T}a_{gt}=u_t^0-O_t+I_t=u_t^L=\nu'_t.
\end{aligned}
\]
Finally,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\pi_{e,t}>0&\ \Longrightarrow\ (e=\varphi(t))\ \lor\ (\exists g\in T:\ e=\varphi(g),\ (g,t)\in\mathcal D),\\
e=\varphi(t)&\ \Longrightarrow\ |e-t|<r<(1+4/A)r,\\
e=\varphi(g),\ (g,t)\in\mathcal D&\ \Longrightarrow\ |e-t|\le|\varphi(g)-g|+|g-t|<r+4r/A=(1+4/A)r.
\end{aligned}
\]

label: lem:three-doubling-weights
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:three-doubling-weights}
For every $d,N\in\mathbb N_+$ and distinct sites $X_1,\ldots,X_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$, there exists $\mu\in\Delta_N^\circ$ satisfying \eqref{eq:doubling} with $D=2^{46d}$.
head: environment
name: Positive Geometry Weights with a Dimension-Only Certificate

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the finite redistribution construction of~\cite{VolbergKonyagin1988}. If $N=1$, set $\mu_1=1$; for every $r>0$, both sums in~\eqref{eq:doubling} equal $1\le2^{46d}$. Suppose $N\ge2$. Put $c\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}4(1+\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb X^N))$, $Y_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}(X_i-X_1)/c$, and $X\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{Y_i:i\in[N]\}$. Then
\[
c>0,\qquad |Y_i-Y_k|=c^{-1}|X_i-X_k|,\qquad \operatorname{diam}(X)=\frac{\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb X^N)}{4(1+\operatorname{diam}(\mathbb X^N))}<\frac14.
\]
Write $\mathcal B(z,t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{y\in\mathbb R^d:|y-z|<t\}$ and $B_X(z,t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} X\cap\mathcal B(z,t)$. Set $A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}16$, $B\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} A^{2d}$, $r_j\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} A^{-j}$ for $j\in\mathbb N_0$, $\sigma\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\min_{i\ne k}|Y_i-Y_k|>0$, and $J\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\min\{j\in\mathbb N_0:r_j<\sigma\}<\infty$.

For $0\le j\le J$, define $S_j^{(0)}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\varnothing$ and, with $\operatorname{dist}(z,\varnothing)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\infty$,
\[
S_j^{(i)}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\begin{cases}S_j^{(i-1)}\cup\{Y_i\},&\operatorname{dist}(Y_i,S_j^{(i-1)})\ge r_j,\\S_j^{(i-1)},&\operatorname{dist}(Y_i,S_j^{(i-1)})<r_j,\end{cases}\qquad i\in[N],\qquad S_j\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} S_j^{(N)}.
\]
For $i<k$ with $Y_i,Y_k\in S_j$, the insertion rule gives $|Y_i-Y_k|\ge r_j$; $Y_i\in S_j$ gives $\operatorname{dist}(Y_i,S_j)=0<r_j$, whereas $Y_i\notin S_j$ gives $\operatorname{dist}(Y_i,S_j)\le\operatorname{dist}(Y_i,S_j^{(i-1)})<r_j$. Consequently,
\[
\min_{z\in S_j}|y-z|<r_j\quad(y\in X),\qquad S_0=\{Y_1\},\qquad r_J<\sigma\Longrightarrow S_J=X.
\]
Set $S_j\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} X$ for $j>J$. For every $j\in\mathbb N_0$, let $\varphi_j(t)$ be the least-indexed minimizer of $e\mapsto|t-e|$ on $S_j$, for $t\in S_{j+1}$. Thus $|t-\varphi_j(t)|<r_j$, and $\varphi_j=\operatorname{Id}_X$ for $j\ge J$. For $e\in S_j$, choose $t\in S_{j+1}$ with $|t-e|<r_{j+1}$; then
\[
|e-\varphi_j(t)|\le|e-t|+|t-\varphi_j(t)|\le2|e-t|<2r_{j+1}=\frac{r_j}{8}<r_j\Longrightarrow\varphi_j(t)=e\Longrightarrow\varphi_j(S_{j+1})=S_j.
\]

Set $\nu_0(Y_1)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}1$; then $\nu_0(Y_1)=1\le B^2\nu_0(Y_1)$. Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:three-weight-transfer} inductively with
\[
(S,T,r,\varphi,\nu)=(S_j,S_{j+1},r_j,\varphi_j,\nu_j)\quad(0\le j<J),\qquad 4r_j/A=4r_{j+1}.
\]
Its conclusions give positive probability weights $\nu_j$ on $S_j$, $0\le j\le J$, satisfying
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-weight-properties}
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{e\in S_j}\nu_j(e)=1,\qquad \nu_j(e)>0,\qquad \nu_j(e)\le B^2\nu_j(e')\quad(e,e'\in S_j,\ |e-e'|<4r_j),\\
B^{-1}\nu_j(\varphi_j(t))\le\nu_{j+1}(t)\le\nu_j(\varphi_j(t))\quad(0\le j<J,\ t\in S_{j+1}),
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
and, for $0\le j<J$, numbers $\pi_j(e,t)\ge0$ satisfying
\[
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\pi_j(e,t)=\nu_j(e),\qquad \sum_{e\in S_j}\pi_j(e,t)=\nu_{j+1}(t),\\
\pi_j(e,t)>0\Longrightarrow|e-t|<Cr_j,\qquad C\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}1+4/A.
\end{gathered}
\]
Put $\mu(y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\nu_J(y)$ for $y\in X$ and $\nu_j\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mu$ for $j\ge J$. Since $r_j\le r_J$, for $e,e'\in X$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
|e-e'|<4r_j\Longrightarrow|e-e'|<4r_J\Longrightarrow\nu_j(e)=\nu_J(e)\le B^2\nu_J(e')=B^2\nu_j(e'),\\
B^{-1}\nu_j(\varphi_j(t))\le\nu_{j+1}(t)=\nu_j(\varphi_j(t)).
\end{gathered}
\]

Set
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-transport-constants}
C_1\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{1+4/A}{1-1/A}=\frac43,\qquad \frac1{1-1/A}=\frac{16}{15},\qquad C+C_1/A=C_1.
\end{equation}
For $j\ge J$, put $\Pi_j(e,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mu(e)\mathbf1_{\{e=y\}}$. For $j=J-1,\ldots,0$, recursively put
\[
\Pi_j(e,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\pi_j(e,t)\frac{\Pi_{j+1}(t,y)}{\nu_{j+1}(t)}\qquad(e\in S_j,\ y\in X).
\]
For $j\ge J$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
\sum_{y\in X}\Pi_j(e,y)=\mu(e)=\nu_j(e),\qquad\sum_{e\in X}\Pi_j(e,y)=\mu(y),\\
\Pi_j(e,y)>0\Longrightarrow e=y\Longrightarrow|e-y|=0<C_1r_j.
\end{gathered}
\]
Since every $\nu_{j+1}(t)>0$, the backward induction step is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{y\in X}\Pi_j(e,y)&=\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\frac{\pi_j(e,t)}{\nu_{j+1}(t)}\sum_{y\in X}\Pi_{j+1}(t,y)=\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\pi_j(e,t)=\nu_j(e),\\
\sum_{e\in S_j}\Pi_j(e,y)&=\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\frac{\Pi_{j+1}(t,y)}{\nu_{j+1}(t)}\sum_{e\in S_j}\pi_j(e,t)=\sum_{t\in S_{j+1}}\Pi_{j+1}(t,y)=\mu(y),\\
\Pi_j(e,y)>0&\Longrightarrow\exists t\in S_{j+1}:\ \pi_j(e,t)\Pi_{j+1}(t,y)>0\\
&\Longrightarrow|e-y|\le|e-t|+|t-y|<Cr_j+C_1r_{j+1}=C_1r_j.
\end{aligned}
\]

Fix $x\in X$ and $r>0$, and write $\mu(E)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{y\in E}\mu(y)$ for $E\subseteq X$. If $r\ge1/2$, then $|y-x|\le\operatorname{diam}(X)<1/4<r$ for every $y\in X$, so $\mu(B_X(x,2r))=\mu(B_X(x,r))=1$. If $0<r<1/2$, put $j_0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\max\{j\in\mathbb N_0:r_j\ge2r\}$ and $j_1\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\min\{j\in\mathbb N_0:r_j\le r\}$. Since $r_0=1>2r>r>0$ and $r_j\downarrow0$, these indices exist with $j_1\ge1$; their extremal properties give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-scale-indices}
\begin{gathered}
r_{j_0}\ge2r>r_{j_0+1}=r_{j_0}/A,\qquad r_{j_1}\le r<r_{j_1-1}=Ar_{j_1},\qquad j_0<j_1,\\
2r\le r_{j_0}<2Ar,\qquad r/A<r_{j_1}\le r,\qquad A^{j_1-j_0}=r_{j_0}/r_{j_1}<2A^2.
\end{gathered}
\end{equation}
Choose $g\in S_{j_1+1}$ with $|g-x|<r_{j_1+1}$, set $g_{j_1+1}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} g$, and recursively set $g_j\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\varphi_j(g_{j+1})$ for $j_0\le j\le j_1$. Then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-ancestor-distance}
|g_{j_0}-x|\le|g-x|+\sum_{j=j_0}^{j_1}|g_j-g_{j+1}|<\sum_{j=j_0}^{j_1+1}r_j\le\frac{r_{j_0}}{1-1/A}.
\end{equation}
Writing $h\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} j_1+1$, we have
\[
\Pi_h(g,y)>0\Longrightarrow|y-x|\le|y-g|+|g-x|<(C_1+1)r_h\le\frac{C_1+1}{A}r=\frac7{48}r<r.
\]
Hence
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-inner-mass}
\mu(B_X(x,r))=\sum_{e\in S_h}\sum_{y\in B_X(x,r)}\Pi_h(e,y)\ge\sum_{y\in B_X(x,r)}\Pi_h(g,y)=\sum_{y\in X}\Pi_h(g,y)=\nu_h(g)>0.
\end{equation}

Set $E_0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{e\in S_{j_0}:|e-x|<2r+C_1r_{j_0}\}$. For $y\in B_X(x,2r)$,
\[
\Pi_{j_0}(e,y)>0\Longrightarrow|e-x|\le|e-y|+|y-x|<C_1r_{j_0}+2r\Longrightarrow e\in E_0.
\]
For $e\in E_0$, \eqref{eq:three-net-scale-indices} and~\eqref{eq:three-net-ancestor-distance} give
\[
|e-g_{j_0}|\le|e-x|+|x-g_{j_0}|<\left(1+C_1+\frac1{1-1/A}\right)r_{j_0}=\frac{17}{5}r_{j_0}<4r_{j_0}.
\]
Since $|e-e'|\ge r_{j_0}$ for distinct $e,e'\in E_0$, the balls $\mathcal B(e,r_{j_0}/2)$ are pairwise disjoint and their union lies in $\mathcal B(g_{j_0},9r_{j_0}/2)$. Thus, with $\omega_d\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}|\mathcal B(0,1)|>0$ denoting Lebesgue volume,
\[
|E_0|\omega_d(r_{j_0}/2)^d=\left|\bigcup_{e\in E_0}\mathcal B(e,r_{j_0}/2)\right|\le\omega_d(9r_{j_0}/2)^d\Longrightarrow|E_0|\le9^d\le12^d.
\]
Consequently, \eqref{eq:three-net-weight-properties} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-net-outer-mass}
\mu(B_X(x,2r))=\sum_{e\in E_0}\sum_{y\in B_X(x,2r)}\Pi_{j_0}(e,y)\le\sum_{e\in E_0}\nu_{j_0}(e)\le12^dB^2\nu_{j_0}(g_{j_0}).
\end{equation}
The parent--child bounds and~\eqref{eq:three-net-scale-indices} imply
\[
\nu_{j_0}(g_{j_0})=\nu_h(g)\prod_{j=j_0}^{h-1}\frac{\nu_j(g_j)}{\nu_{j+1}(g_{j+1})}\le B^{h-j_0}\nu_h(g),\qquad B^{j_1-j_0}=\bigl(A^{j_1-j_0}\bigr)^{2d}\le2^{2d}B^2.
\]
Using~\eqref{eq:three-net-inner-mass} and~\eqref{eq:three-net-outer-mass}, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-dimension-doubling-certificate}
\begin{aligned}
\mu(B_X(x,2r))&\le12^dB^{j_1-j_0+3}\nu_h(g)\\
&\le12^dB^5 2^{2d}\mu(B_X(x,r))=\left(\frac34\right)^d2^{46d}\mu(B_X(x,r))\le2^{46d}\mu(B_X(x,r)).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Finally, set $\mu_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mu(Y_i)$ for $i\in[N]$. Then $\mu_i>0$, $\sum_i\mu_i=1$, and, for every $i\in[N]$ and $\rho>0$,
\[
\sum_{\substack{k\in[N]\\|X_k-X_i|<2\rho}}\mu_k=\mu(B_X(Y_i,2\rho/c))\le2^{46d}\mu(B_X(Y_i,\rho/c))=2^{46d}\sum_{\substack{k\in[N]\\|X_k-X_i|<\rho}}\mu_k.
\]

label: lem:finite-whitney-seminorm
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:finite-whitney-seminorm}
    Fix $d,N\in\mathbb N_+$ and $s\in\mathbb N$. Let
    $X_1,\ldots,X_N\in\mathbb{R}^d$ be distinct, and let
    $P_1,\ldots,P_N$ be real polynomials of degree at most $s$.
    For these data $\mathbb{D}^N\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\{(X_i,P_i)\}_{i=1}^N$, define $W_{\mathbb{D}^N}$ as in~\eqref{eq:finite-whitney-seminorm}.
    There is a constant $\kappa_{d,s}\ge1$, depending only on $d,s$,
    such that:
    \begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)] Every $f\in\dot{C}^{s,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with
    $J_{X_i}^sf=P_i$ for all $i\in[N]$ satisfies
    $W_{\mathbb{D}^N}\le[f]_{s,1}$.
    \item[(ii)] There exists $g\in\dot{C}^{s,1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ with
    $J_{X_i}^sg=P_i$ for all $i\in[N]$ and
    $[g]_{s,1}\le\kappa_{d,s}W_{\mathbb{D}^N}$.
    \item[(iii)] $W_{\mathbb{D}^N}=0$ if and only if all $P_i$
    are the same polynomial. In that case one may take $g=P_1$.
    \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Finite-Jet seminorm

title: Proof
body_md:
For (i), the assertion is immediate from the definition when $N=1$.
    For $i\ne j$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, apply
    Lemma~\ref{lem:three-taylor} to $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$, with base
    point $X_i$, evaluation point $X_j$, and derivative order $|\alpha|$.
    Since $D^{|\alpha|}P_j(X_j)=D^{|\alpha|}f(X_j)$ and a coordinate
    component is bounded by the operator norm, this gives
    \[
     |\partial^\alpha(P_i-P_j)(X_j)|
     \le \frac{[f]_{s,1}}{(s+1-|\alpha|)!}
           |X_i-X_j|^{s+1-|\alpha|}
     \le [f]_{s,1}|X_i-X_j|^{s+1-|\alpha|}.
    \]
    Division by the positive denominator and maximization prove (i).
    
    If $W_{\mathbb{D}^N}=0$ and $N\ge2$, every derivative through
    order $s$ of $P_i-P_j$ vanishes at $X_j$. The exact Taylor
    expansion of this polynomial, whose degree is at most $s$, is
    therefore zero. Hence $P_i=P_j$. The assertion for $N=1$ is
    automatic, and the converse follows directly from the definition.
    A polynomial of degree at most $s$ has constant order-$s$
    derivative and thus has seminorm zero. This proves (iii) and
    also proves (ii) when $W_{\mathbb{D}^N}=0$.
    
    Suppose $W\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} W_{\mathbb{D}^N}>0$. Then $N\ge2$, and
    \[
     a\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} X_1,\qquad
     R\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\max_{i\in[N]}|X_i-a|>0,\qquad
     z_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{X_i-a}{R},\qquad
     Q_i(z)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{P_i(a+Rz)-P_1(a+Rz)}{WR^{s+1}}
    \]
    are well defined. Regard $Q_i$, of degree at most $s$, as an
    $(s+1)$-jet at $z_i$; its derivatives of order $s+1$ are zero.
    For $i\ne1$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, the ordered pair $(1,i)$ in~\eqref{eq:finite-whitney-seminorm} yields
    \[
     |\partial^\alpha Q_i(z_i)|
     =\frac{|\partial^\alpha(P_i-P_1)(X_i)|}
            {WR^{s+1-|\alpha|}}
     \le\left(\frac{|X_i-a|}{R}\right)^{s+1-|\alpha|}
     \le1.
    \]
    For $i=1$, this inequality holds because $Q_1=0$; for
    $|\alpha|=s+1$, it holds because the derivative is zero.
    For $i\ne j$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, one also has
    \[
     |\partial^\alpha(Q_i-Q_j)(z_j)|
     =\frac{|\partial^\alpha(P_i-P_j)(X_j)|}
            {WR^{s+1-|\alpha|}}
     \le |z_i-z_j|^{s+1-|\alpha|}.
    \]
    When $i=j$ the difference is zero; when $|\alpha|=s+1$
    both derivatives vanish. Thus all the hypotheses of
    \cite[Lemma~3.6, p.~327]{Fefferman2006} hold with
    $n=d$, $m=s+1$, $S=\{z_i:i\in[N]\}$, $P^{z_i}=Q_i$,
    and $A=1$. The sites remain distinct under the rescaling.
    That lemma supplies $H\in C^{s+1}(\mathbb{R}^d)$ satisfying
    \[
     J_{z_i}^{s+1}H=Q_i\quad(i\in[N]),\qquad
     \max_{|\alpha|\le s+1}
     \sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^d}|\partial^\alpha H(z)|
     \le B_{d,s},
    \]
    where $B_{d,s}\ge1$ depends only on $d,s$. Here any fixed
    conversion from the source's $C^{s+1}$ norm to the displayed
    maximum is absorbed in $B_{d,s}$.
    For unit vectors $u_1,\ldots,u_{s+1}$, expansion in coordinates
    and the inequality $\sum_{k=1}^d|(u_\ell)_k|\le\sqrt d$ give
    \[
     |D^{s+1}H(z)[u_1,\ldots,u_{s+1}]|
     \le B_{d,s}\prod_{\ell=1}^{s+1}
                  \sum_{k=1}^d|(u_\ell)_k|
     \le d^{(s+1)/2}B_{d,s}.
    \]
    Set $\kappa_{d,s}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} d^{(s+1)/2}B_{d,s}$ and
    $
     g(x)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} P_1(x)+WR^{s+1}H\!\left(\frac{x-a}{R}\right)
    $.
    For every $i\in[N]$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, the chain rule and
    the jet identity for $H$ give
    \[
     \partial^\alpha g(X_i)
     =\partial^\alpha P_1(X_i)
      +WR^{s+1-|\alpha|}\partial^\alpha Q_i(z_i)
     =\partial^\alpha P_i(X_i).
    \]
    Thus $J_{X_i}^sg=P_i$. Since $D^{s+1}P_1=0$, the same
    chain rule yields
    $\sup_x\|D^{s+1}g(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\kappa_{d,s}W$.
    For $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$, integration along their segment gives
    \[
     D^sg(y)-D^sg(x)
     =\int_0^1D^{s+1}g(x+t(y-x))[y-x,\,\cdot\,]\,\mathrm dt,
    \]
    where the expression is scalar when $s=0$. Taking operator
    norms gives
    \[
     \|D^sg(y)-D^sg(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\kappa_{d,s}W|y-x|.
    \]
    This proves (ii).

body_md:
For $s=0$ one has $\mathcal I_0=\{1\}$, $\beta=0$, $p=m=1$, $A_s=1$, and $P_i(x)=f(X_i)$. Hence $F=F_1$, the variance coefficient vanishes because it contains the factor $s=0$, and the entropy coefficient vanishes because $\beta=0$. 
                                                                                                             
Off the sites $\{X_i\}_{i=1}^N$, the objective defining $F_1$ in~\eqref{eq:entropy-variance-extension__primal} is consequently a convex combination
of the finitely many numbers $f(X_i)+M|x-X_i|$. Every such combination is at least their minimum, and a simplex vertex attaining that minimum realizes equality. At $x=X_n$, \eqref{eq:training_data} gives $f(X_i)+M|X_n-X_i|\ge f(X_n)$ for every $i$, with equality at $i=n$. Hence \eqref{eq:three-zero-envelope} also equals the assigned value at each site.
For arbitrary $x,y\in\mathbb{R}^d$, choose an index $i$ minimizing \eqref{eq:three-zero-envelope} at $y$. Then
\[
 F(x)-F(y)\le M\bigl(|x-X_i|-|y-X_i|\bigr)\le M|x-y|.
\]
Choosing instead an index minimizing at $x$ gives $F(y)-F(x)\le M|x-y|$. Thus $|F(x)-F(y)|\le M|x-y|$, which proves the asserted Lipschitz bound and continuity, including at the sites.

label: eq:three-grouped-envelope
title: Proof
body_md:
Define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-grouped-envelope}
H(x)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\inf\left\{\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(y_i):\lambda\in\Delta_N,\ (y_i)_{i=1}^N\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^N,\ \sum_i\lambda_i y_i=x\right\}.
\end{equation}
Put $\ell_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} G_i-MX_i$, $c_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} f_i-G_i\cdot X_i+\frac M2|X_i|^2$, and $B\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\max\{0,\max_i(|\ell_i|^2/(2M)-c_i)\}$. Then
\[
g_i(y)=M|y|^2+\ell_i\cdot y+c_i=\frac M2|y|^2+\frac M2\left|y+\frac{\ell_i}{M}\right|^2+c_i-\frac{|\ell_i|^2}{2M}\ge\frac M2|y|^2-B.
\]
For every admissible $(\lambda,(y_i))$, the identity $\sum_i\lambda_i|y_i|^2=|x|^2+\sum_i\lambda_i|y_i-x|^2$ gives
\[
\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(y_i)\ge\frac M2|x|^2+\frac M2\sum_i\lambda_i|y_i-x|^2-B\ge\frac M2|x|^2-B.
\]
Taking $\lambda=e_j$ and $y_i=x$ for every $i$ also gives $H(x)\le g_j(x)$; hence $\frac M2|x|^2-B\le H(x)\le g(x)<\infty$.
Fix $x,x'\in\mathbb{R}^d$, $t\in(0,1)$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Choose admissible $(\lambda,(y_i))$ and $(\lambda',(y_i'))$ at $x$ and $x'$, respectively, with $\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(y_i)\le H(x)+\varepsilon$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i'g_i(y_i')\le H(x')+\varepsilon$. Set
\[
\widehat\lambda_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} t\lambda_i+(1-t)\lambda_i',\qquad
\widehat y_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle\frac{t\lambda_i y_i+(1-t)\lambda_i'y_i'}{\widehat\lambda_i},&\widehat\lambda_i>0,\\
0,&\widehat\lambda_i=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $\widehat\lambda_i\ge0$, $\sum_i\widehat\lambda_i=t+(1-t)=1$, and
\[
\sum_i\widehat\lambda_i\widehat y_i=t\sum_i\lambda_i y_i+(1-t)\sum_i\lambda_i'y_i'=tx+(1-t)x'.
\]
For every $i\in[N]$,
\[
t\lambda_i g_i(y_i)+(1-t)\lambda_i'g_i(y_i')-\widehat\lambda_i g_i(\widehat y_i)
=M\bigl(t\lambda_i|y_i-\widehat y_i|^2+(1-t)\lambda_i'|y_i'-\widehat y_i|^2\bigr)\ge0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(tx+(1-t)x')&\le\sum_i\widehat\lambda_i g_i(\widehat y_i)\\
&\le t\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(y_i)+(1-t)\sum_i\lambda_i'g_i(y_i')\\
&\le tH(x)+(1-t)H(x')+\varepsilon.
\end{aligned}
\]
Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves convexity; the cases $t=0,1$ are equalities.

Fix $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $r>0$. Set $V\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} x+r\{-1,1\}^d$ and $A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\max_{v\in V}H(v)$. Since $x+[-r,r]^d$ is the convex hull of $V$, convexity gives $H\le A$ on this cube. For $0<\|h\|_\infty<r$, put $t\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\|h\|_\infty/r$ and $u_\pm\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} x\pm h/t$. Then $u_\pm\in x+[-r,r]^d$ and
$
x+h=(1-t)x+tu_+$ implies that $H(x+h)\le(1-t)H(x)+tA$; while 
$x=\frac{x+h}{1+t}+\frac{t}{1+t}u_-$ implies that $H(x)\le\frac{H(x+h)+tA}{1+t}$.  
Thus $|H(x+h)-H(x)|\le r^{-1}(A-H(x))\|h\|_\infty\to0$ as $h\to0$, so $H$ is continuous. If $u:\mathbb{R}^d\to\mathbb{R}$ is any lower-semicontinuous convex minorant of $g$, every admissible representation gives
\[
u(x)\le\sum_i\lambda_i u(y_i)\le\sum_i\lambda_i g(y_i)\le\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(y_i).
\]
Taking the infimum yields $u\le H$. Since $H$ is itself a continuous convex minorant of $g$, $H=\operatorname{conv}(g)$.

Fix $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$ and $\lambda\in\Delta_N$. Write $y_i=x+h_i$ and $\bar v\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_i\lambda_i v_i(x)$, so that $\sum_i\lambda_i y_i=x$ is equivalent to $\sum_i\lambda_i h_i=0$. Under this constraint,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-quadratic-expansion}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x+h_i)
&=\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i\bigl((v_i(x)+Mx)\cdot h_i+M|h_i|^2\bigr)\\
&=\sum_i\lambda_i\left(P_i(x)+\frac M2|x-X_i|^2\right)+\frac M2|x|^2+\sum_i\lambda_i\bigl(v_i(x)\cdot h_i+M|h_i|^2\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The identities $\sum_i\lambda_i(v_i(x)-\bar v)=0$, $\sum_i\lambda_i\bar v\cdot h_i=0$, and $\operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v(x))=\sum_i\lambda_i|v_i(x)-\bar v|^2$ give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-variance-completion}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\lambda_i\bigl(v_i(x)\cdot h_i+M|h_i|^2\bigr)
&=M\sum_i\lambda_i\left|h_i+\frac{v_i(x)-\bar v}{2M}\right|^2-\frac1{4M}\operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v(x)).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For $h_i^*\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}-(v_i(x)-\bar v)/(2M)$, one has $\sum_i\lambda_i h_i^*=-(\sum_i\lambda_i v_i(x)-\bar v)/(2M)=0$, and every square in \eqref{eq:three-variance-completion} vanishes. Therefore,
\[
\inf_{\substack{(h_i)\in(\mathbb{R}^d)^N\\ \sum_i\lambda_i h_i=0}}\sum_i\lambda_i g_i(x+h_i)
=\sum_i\lambda_i\left(P_i(x)+\frac M2|x-X_i|^2\right)+\frac M2|x|^2-\frac1{4M}\operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v(x)).
\]
The right-hand side is polynomial in $\lambda$, and $\Delta_N$ is nonempty and compact. Taking its minimum over $\Delta_N$ in \eqref{eq:three-grouped-envelope}, and using $H=\operatorname{conv}(g)$, proves \eqref{eq:three-variance-envelope-identity}.

label: eq:three-boundary-variation
title: Proof
body_md:
The objective is continuous on $\Delta_N$. A minimizing sequence has a coordinatewise convergent subsequence in $[0,1]^N$; its limit belongs to $\Delta_N$ and attains the infimum by continuity. Suppose a minimizer has $\lambda_j=0$ and $\lambda_k=L>0$. Put $z=\sum_i\lambda_i b_i$ and $d_b=b_j-b_k$. Replace these coordinates by $\varepsilon$ and $L-\varepsilon$, with $0<\varepsilon<L/2$. The change in the objective is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-boundary-variation}
 \varepsilon(w_j-w_k)+2c\varepsilon z\cdot d_b+c\varepsilon^2|d_b|^2
 +\varepsilon\log(\varepsilon/\theta_j)
 +(L-\varepsilon)\log((L-\varepsilon)/\theta_k)-L\log(L/\theta_k).
\end{equation}
Set $B=\max_{r\in[L/2,L]}|1+\log(r/\theta_k)|$ and
$C=|w_j-w_k|+2c|z||d_b|+c|d_b|^2+|\log\theta_j|+B$.
The fundamental theorem of calculus bounds \eqref{eq:three-boundary-variation} above by $\varepsilon\log\varepsilon+C\varepsilon$ whenever $\varepsilon<1$. Taking $\varepsilon<\min\{L/2,1,\mathrm{e}^{-C-1}\}$ contradicts minimality. On the interior, the Hessian of the entropy is $\operatorname{diag}(1/\lambda_i)$, while the quadratic term is convex. Strict convexity along every nonconstant segment in the interior proves uniqueness.

At an interior minimizer the derivatives in every feasible direction $e_i-e_j$ vanish. Thus all partial derivatives of the objective are equal, giving
$ w_i+2cz_*\cdot b_i+\log(\lambda_i^*/\theta_i)+1=\text{constant}$,
which proves the first line of \eqref{eq:three-gibbs-dual}. To justify the second line without a minimax interchange, let
$Z(z)=\sum_i\theta_i \mathrm{e}^{-w_i-2cz\cdot b_i}$ and
$\pi_i(z)=\theta_i \mathrm{e}^{-w_i-2cz\cdot b_i}/Z(z)$.
For every $\lambda\in\Delta_N$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-duality-gap}
 \sum_i\lambda_i w_i+c\left|\sum_i\lambda_i b_i\right|^2
 +\operatorname{KL}(\lambda\mid\theta)
 =-c|z|^2-\log Z(z)
 +c\left|\sum_i\lambda_i b_i-z\right|^2
 +\operatorname{KL}(\lambda\mid\pi(z)).
\end{equation}
The relative entropy is nonnegative: $\log t\le t-1$ gives
$\sum_{\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i\log(\pi_i/\lambda_i)
\le\sum_{\lambda_i>0}\pi_i-1\le0$.
Equality in \eqref{eq:three-duality-gap} holds for $z=z_*$ and $\lambda=\lambda^*$. This proves duality and attainment.

Write $\bar b(z)=\sum_i\pi_i(z)b_i$ and define
$\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi(z)}(b)=\sum_i\pi_i(z)(b_i-\bar b(z))(b_i-\bar b(z))^\top$.
Differentiating the finite sum gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-dual-hessian}
 \nabla_z(-c|z|^2-\log Z(z))=-2c(z-\bar b(z)),\qquad
 D_z^2(-c|z|^2-\log Z(z))=-2cI-4c^2\operatorname{Cov}_{\pi(z)}(b).
\end{equation}
Here $v^\top\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(b)v=\sum_i\pi_i(v\cdot(b_i-\bar b))^2\ge0$. Thus the dual is strictly concave and its maximizer is unique. The stationarity map $K=z-\bar b$ has $D_zK=I+2c\operatorname{Cov}_\pi(b)$. For every vector $u$, $u^\top D_zK\,u\ge|u|^2$, so Cauchy-Schwarz gives $|D_zK\,u|\ge|u|$. This square matrix is injective and therefore invertible, and its inverse has norm at most one.

We record the local smoothness argument used here and later. Let $K(x_0,z_0)=0$ and let $J=D_zK(x_0,z_0)$ be invertible. Write $\Phi_x(z)=z-J^{-1}K(x,z)$. By continuity of $D_zK$, there are convex parameter and $z$ neighborhoods with compact closures on which $\left\lVertD_z\Phi_x(z)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}\le1/2$. Choose a closed ball of radius $r>0$ about $z_0$ in the latter neighborhood, and shrink the parameter neighborhood until $|\Phi_x(z_0)-z_0|\le r/2$. The derivative bound, integrated on a segment, gives $|\Phi_x(z)-\Phi_x(z')|\le|z-z'|/2$ in the ball. Hence $\Phi_x$ maps the ball to itself. Its iterates from $z_0$ have successive differences at most $2^{-n}$ times the first difference, so they are Cauchy. Their limit is a fixed point by continuity and is unique in the ball by the same contraction inequality.

Let $A$ bound $\left\lVertD_x\Phi_x(z)\right\rVert_{\mathrm{op}}$ on this compact product. For two parameters in the chosen convex neighborhood, their fixed points satisfy
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-implicit-local-Lipschitz}
 |z(x)-z(x')|\le\tfrac12|z(x)-z(x')|+A|x-x'|,
 \qquad |z(x)-z(x')|\le2A|x-x'|.
\end{equation}
Put $\Delta z=z(x+\eta)-z(x)$. Differentiability of $K$ and \eqref{eq:three-implicit-local-Lipschitz} give
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 0&=D_xK(x,z(x))\eta+D_zK(x,z(x))\Delta z+o(|\eta|+|\Delta z|)\\
  &=D_xK(x,z(x))\eta+D_zK(x,z(x))\Delta z+o(|\eta|).
 \end{aligned}
\]
Here $D_zK$ remains invertible: $J^{-1}D_zK=I-D_z\Phi_x$ and the inverse of $I-D_z\Phi_x$ is its convergent geometric matrix series. Solving the last expansion proves
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-implicit-derivative}
 Dz(x)=-(D_zK(x,z(x)))^{-1}D_xK(x,z(x)).
\end{equation}
The right side is continuous, so $z$ is $C^1$. Matrix inversion is smooth where the determinant is nonzero, by the adjugate formula. If $z$ is $C^k$, the right side of \eqref{eq:three-implicit-derivative} is $C^k$, since $K$ is smooth; hence $z$ is $C^{k+1}$. Induction gives smoothness of every finite order. The local fixed points solve the stationarity equation and therefore equal the unique global maximizer by \eqref{eq:three-dual-hessian}. The Gibbs formula then proves smoothness of the weights and optimal value.

label: eq:three-variance-translation
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x$ in the neighborhood under consideration and $\lambda\in\Delta_N$. Translation invariance of weighted variance follows by expanding its definition:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-variance-translation}
 \operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v-\nabla Q)
 =\sum_i\lambda_i|v_i-\nabla Q|^2
 -\left|\sum_i\lambda_i(v_i-\nabla Q)\right|^2
 =\operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v),
\end{equation}
where $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$. By~\eqref{eq:three-normalized-data},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-variance-scaling}
 \operatorname{Var}_\lambda\bigl(b^{(\vartheta)}(x)\bigr)
 =\frac{\vartheta}{M^2R(x)^{2s}}
 \operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v(x)).
\end{equation}
Moreover,
$
 \sum_i\lambda_i|b_i^{(\vartheta)}|^2
 -\left|\sum_i\lambda_i b_i^{(\vartheta)}\right|^2
 =\operatorname{Var}_\lambda\bigl(b^{(\vartheta)}\bigr)$.  
Multiplying the objective in~\eqref{eq:three-abstract-primal} by $\beta MR(x)^m$ and adding $Q(x)$ gives
\begin{align*}
 &Q(x)+\beta MR(x)^m
 \left[
 \sum_i\lambda_iw_i^{(\vartheta)}(x)
 +c\left|\sum_i\lambda_i b_i^{(\vartheta)}(x)\right|^2
 +\operatorname{KL}(\lambda\mid\theta(x))
 \right]\\
 &\quad=Q(x)+\sum_i\lambda_i(P_i(x)-Q(x))
 +\sum_i\lambda_i\frac{A_sM r_i(x)^{2s}}{R(x)^{s-1}}\\
 &\qquad\quad
 -\beta cMR(x)^m
 \operatorname{Var}_\lambda\bigl(b^{(\vartheta)}(x)\bigr)
 +\beta MR(x)^m\operatorname{KL}(\lambda\mid\theta(x))\\
 &\quad=\sum_i\lambda_i
 \left[P_i(x)+\frac{A_sM r_i(x)^{2s}}{R(x)^{s-1}}\right]
 -\frac{\vartheta s}{4MR(x)^{s-1}}
 \operatorname{Var}_\lambda(v(x))
 +(s-1)MR(x)^{s+1}\operatorname{KL}(\lambda\mid\theta(x)).
\end{align*}
Here $m=s+1$, $\beta=s-1$, $\beta c=s/4$, and~\eqref{eq:three-variance-scaling} were used in the last equality. Taking the minimum over $\lambda\in\Delta_N$ proves~\eqref{eq:three-F-normalized}. No division by $\vartheta$ or $\sqrt\vartheta$ occurs. Lemma~\ref{lem:three-entropy} applies because the auxiliary coefficient $c=s/[4(s-1)]$ remains strictly positive and every $\theta_i$ is positive.

At $x_0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:three-taylor}, first with derivative order zero and then with order one, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-base-remainders}
 |\delta_i(x_0)|\le\frac{t_i^m}{m!},
 \qquad
 \left|b_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)\right|
 \le\sqrt\vartheta\,\frac{2t_i^s}{s!}
 \le\frac{2t_i^s}{s!},
 \qquad
 t_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{r_i(x_0)}{R(x_0)}.
\end{equation}
Since $2/s!\le1$, the vector bound in~\eqref{eq:three-normalized-bounds} follows. Also
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-a-lower-general}
 w_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)
 \ge
 \left(
 \frac12+\frac1{\beta m!}
 -\frac{\vartheta s}{\beta(s!)^2}
 \right)t_i^{2s}
 -\frac{t_i^m}{\beta m!}.
\end{equation}
When $s=2$, this gives the endpoint estimate
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-s-two-parameter-bound}
 w_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)
 \ge-\frac{t_i^3}{6}
 +\left(\frac23-\frac\vartheta2\right)t_i^4
 \ge-\frac{t_i^3}{6}+\frac{t_i^4}{6}.
\end{equation}
The polynomial $t^4/12-t^3/6$ has minimum $-9/64$ on $[0,\infty)$, attained at $t=3/2$; its derivative is $t^2(2t-3)/6$. Hence~\eqref{eq:three-s-two-parameter-bound} yields $w_i^{(\vartheta)}\ge t_i^4/12-9/64\ge u_i^2/12-1$. For $s\ge3$, the coefficient in~\eqref{eq:three-a-lower-general} is bounded below by its value at $\vartheta=1$. The inequality $t_i^m\le1+t_i^{2s}$ follows by treating $t_i\le1$ and $t_i\ge1$ separately. The positive sequences $s/((s-1)(s!)^2)$ and $1/((s-1)(s+1)!)$ decrease: their consecutive ratios are $(s-1)/(s^2(s+1))$ and $(s-1)/(s(s+2))$, both less than one. At $s=3$ their values are $1/24$ and $1/48$, respectively. Substitution into~\eqref{eq:three-a-lower-general} gives $w_i^{(\vartheta)}\ge(11/24)t_i^{2s}-1/48\ge u_i^2/12-1$. Dropping the nonpositive term $-c|b_i^{(\vartheta)}|^2$ and using $t_i^m\le1+t_i^{2s}$ gives
\[
 w_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)
 \le\frac1{\beta m!}
 +\left(\frac12+\frac2{\beta m!}\right)t_i^{2s}
 \le1+t_i^{2s}.
\]
The moment identity for $\theta$ follows from the definition of $R$.

The lower cost bound, the nonnegativity of the quadratic term, and the nonnegativity of relative entropy give $\mathfrak h_\vartheta(x_0)\ge-1$. At $\lambda=\theta(x_0)$, evaluate the unexpanded normalized family objective and retain its nonpositive variance term. The inequality
\[
 \sum_i\theta_i t_i^m
 \le\left(\sum_i\theta_i t_i^{2s}\right)^{m/(2s)}=1
\]
follows from concavity of $t\mapsto t^{m/(2s)}$ and finite Jensen. Therefore
\[
 \mathfrak h_\vartheta(x_0)
 \le\frac{A_s}{\beta}+\frac1{\beta m!}
 =\frac12+\frac2{\beta m!}\le\frac56.
\]
At the optimizer,
\[
 c|z_{0,\vartheta}|^2
 \le\mathfrak h_\vartheta(x_0)+1\le\frac{11}{6}.
\]
Since $c\ge1/4$, this proves $|z_{0,\vartheta}|<3$. At $\vartheta=0$, the definition gives $b_i^{(0)}\equiv0$, and hence its weighted mean is $z_{0,0}=0$.

The Gibbs exponent satisfies
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-exponent-tail}
 w_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)
 +2c z_{0,\vartheta}\cdot b_i^{(\vartheta)}(x_0)
 \ge\frac{u_i^2}{12}-1-3u_i
 \ge\frac{u_i^2}{24}-55.
\end{equation}
Indeed, $2c\le1$, $|z_{0,\vartheta}|<3$, and $|b_i^{(\vartheta)}|\le u_i$; the last inequality uses $u^2/24-3u\ge-54$. The identity $\sum_i\theta_i u_i^2=1$ implies that the set $u_i^2\le2$ has $\theta$-mass at least $1/2$. On that set the exponent is at most $3+3\sqrt2<8$. Therefore its partition function is at least $\mathrm e^{-8}/2$. The first line of~\eqref{eq:three-gibbs-dual} and~\eqref{eq:three-exponent-tail} give
\[
 \pi_i^{(\vartheta)}
 \le2\mathrm e^{63}\theta_i\mathrm e^{-u_i^2/24}
 \le\mathrm e^{64}\theta_i\mathrm e^{-u_i^2/24}.
\]
Finally, for $k\ge1$, the maximum of $(1+v)^k\mathrm e^{-v/24}$ on $v\ge0$ is $(24k)^k\mathrm e^{-k+1/24}\le\mathrm e(24k)^k$. Thus
\[
 \sum_i\pi_i^{(\vartheta)}V_i^k
 \le\mathrm e^{65}(24k)^k.
\]
The bound $k!\ge(k/\mathrm e)^k$ follows from
$\sum_{j=1}^k\log j\ge\int_1^k\log t\,\mathrm d t=k\log k-k+1$. This proves~\eqref{eq:three-moment-bound} uniformly in $\vartheta$.

label: def:three-majorization
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:three-majorization}
Let $(E,\|\cdot\|_E)$ be a finite-dimensional normed real vector space, let $U\subseteq\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^d$ be an open neighborhood of $(0,0)$, and let $G\in C^\infty(U;E)$. For $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$, the mixed derivative $\partial_t^jD_y^kG(0,0)$ is an $E$-valued symmetric $k$-linear map on $(\mathbb{R}^d)^k$. For $k\ge1$, equip this map with the operator norm
\[
 \bigl\|\partial_t^jD_y^kG(0,0)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
 \sup_{\substack{h_1,\ldots,h_k\in\mathbb{R}^d\\|h_1|,\ldots,|h_k|\le1}}
 \bigl\|\partial_t^jD_y^kG(0,0)[h_1,\ldots,h_k]\bigr\|_E.
\]
For $k=0$, set $D_y^0G\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} G$ and interpret $\|\partial_t^jD_y^0G(0,0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ as $\|\partial_t^jG(0,0)\|_E$. Thus the same notation covers scalar-valued, vector-valued, and tensor-valued maps by choosing the corresponding finite-dimensional normed codomain $E$.

An $E$-valued formal series in two indeterminates is a family $(A_{jk})_{j,k\in\mathbb N_0}\subseteq E$, written
\[
 A(t,v)=\sum_{j,k\ge0}A_{jk}t^jv^k.
\]
A scalar formal majorant is a series
\[
 B(t,v)=\sum_{j,k\ge0}B_{jk}t^jv^k,
 \qquad B_{jk}\in[0,\infty).
\]
For either series, write $[t^jv^k]A\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} A_{jk}$ and $[t^jv^k]B\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} B_{jk}$. In these expressions, $t$ and $v$ are formal indeterminates; in particular, no convergence of either series is assumed.

For $n\in\mathbb N_0$, define the truncated coefficientwise relations
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-majorization-definition}
\begin{aligned}
 A\preccurlyeq_n B
 &\quad\text{when}\quad
 \bigl\|[t^jv^k]A\bigr\|_E
 \le [t^jv^k]B
 &&\text{for every }j,k\in\mathbb N_0\text{ with }j+k\le n,\\
 G\preccurlyeq_n B
 &\quad\text{when}\quad
 \frac{\bigl\|\partial_t^jD_y^kG(0,0)\bigr\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{j!\,k!}
 \le [t^jv^k]B
 &&\text{for every }j,k\in\mathbb N_0\text{ with }j+k\le n.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
We write $A\preccurlyeq B$ when $A\preccurlyeq_n B$ for every $n\in\mathbb N_0$, and we write $G\preccurlyeq B$ when $G\preccurlyeq_n B$ for every $n\in\mathbb N_0$. When $E=\mathbb{R}$, the norm $\|\cdot\|_E$ in the formal-series relation is absolute value.

If $G$ depends only on the scalar variable $t$ and $B(t)=\sum_{j\ge0}B_jt^j$, then $G\preccurlyeq_n B$ means
\[
 \frac{\|\partial_t^jG(0)\|_E}{j!}\le B_j,
 \qquad 0\le j\le n,
\]
and $G\preccurlyeq B$ means that these inequalities hold for every $j\in\mathbb N_0$. This is precisely the specialization of~\eqref{eq:three-majorization-definition} to $k=0$. The same convention applies to one-variable formal series.

body_md: The relation $G\preccurlyeq_n B$ depends only on the order-$n$ Taylor jet of $G$ at $(0,0)$ and is therefore defined whenever $G$ is of class $C^n$ near $(0,0)$. The untruncated notation $G\preccurlyeq B$ requires derivatives of every finite order, but does not assert that the Taylor series of $G$ converges or represents $G$\footnote{Likewise, the formal relation $A\preccurlyeq B$ is purely coefficientwise; whenever a later argument evaluates $A$ or $B$ at positive numerical arguments, convergence at those arguments must be established separately.}.

title: Proof
body_md:
For a smooth map $K$ with values in a finite-dimensional normed space, and for $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$, set
\[
 \mathfrak c_{j,k}(K)
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
 \frac{\|\partial_t^jD_y^kK(0,0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{j!\,k!}.
\]
Thus $K\preccurlyeq A=\sum_{j,k\ge0}A_{jk}t^jv^k$ means precisely that $\mathfrak c_{j,k}(K)\le A_{jk}$ for every $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$. We prove the three assertions coefficient by coefficient.

Suppose first that $G,H$ take values in the same normed space and satisfy $G\preccurlyeq B$ and $H\preccurlyeq C$. The triangle inequality gives $\mathfrak c_{j,k}(G+H)\le B_{jk}+C_{jk}=[t^jv^k](B+C)$ for every $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$. Hence $G+H\preccurlyeq B+C$.

We next prove the bilinear-product assertion. Let $E_1,E_2,E_3$ be finite-dimensional normed spaces, let $\mathfrak m:E_1\times E_2\to E_3$ be bilinear, and suppose
\[
 \|\mathfrak m(x_1,x_2)\|_{E_3}
 \le \|x_1\|_{E_1}\|x_2\|_{E_2},
 \qquad x_1\in E_1,\quad x_2\in E_2.
\]
Write $K\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mathfrak m(G,H)$. Fix $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$ and vectors $h_1,\ldots,h_k\in\mathbb{R}^d$. For a subset $I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_r\}\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}$, write $h_I\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}(h_{i_1},\ldots,h_{i_r})$; for $I=\varnothing$, the corresponding derivative is the order-zero derivative. The mixed Leibniz rule gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-majorant-mixed-Leibniz}
 \partial_t^jD_y^kK(0,0)[h_1,\ldots,h_k]
 =
 \sum_{a=0}^j\binom ja
 \sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,k\}}
 \mathfrak m\!\left(
 \partial_t^aD_y^{|I|}G(0,0)[h_I],
 \partial_t^{j-a}D_y^{k-|I|}H(0,0)[h_{I^c}]
 \right).
\end{equation}
Indeed, one first distributes the $j$ derivatives in the scalar variable between the two factors, producing the factor $\binom ja$, and then distributes the labelled $y$-directions $h_1,\ldots,h_k$ between the two factors, producing the sum over subsets $I$.

Assume now that $|h_1|,\ldots,|h_k|\le1$. Applying the bilinear bound in~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-mixed-Leibniz}, taking the supremum over these vectors, grouping the subsets according to $b=|I|$, and using $G\preccurlyeq B$ and $H\preccurlyeq C$, we obtain
\begin{align*}
 \|\partial_t^jD_y^kK(0,0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 &\le
 \sum_{a=0}^j\binom ja
 \sum_{b=0}^k\binom kb
 \|\partial_t^aD_y^bG(0,0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \|\partial_t^{j-a}D_y^{k-b}H(0,0)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\\
 &\le
 \sum_{a=0}^j\sum_{b=0}^k
 \binom ja\binom kb
 a!\,b!\,B_{ab}
 (j-a)!\,(k-b)!\,C_{j-a,k-b}\\
 &=j!\,k!
 \sum_{a=0}^j\sum_{b=0}^k
 B_{ab}C_{j-a,k-b}.
\end{align*}
Consequently,
\[
 \mathfrak c_{j,k}(K)
 \le
 \sum_{a=0}^j\sum_{b=0}^kB_{ab}C_{j-a,k-b}
 =
 [t^jv^k](BC).
\]
Since $j,k$ were arbitrary, $\mathfrak m(G,H)\preccurlyeq BC$. This proves the addition and bilinear-product assertions.

We next prove~\eqref{eq:three-analytic-majorants}. Let $G$ be scalar valued, assume $G(0,0)=0$, and suppose $G\preccurlyeq B$ with $B_{00}=0$. Repeated application of the bilinear-product estimate gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-majorant-powers}
 G^m\preccurlyeq B^m,
 \qquad m\in\mathbb N_0,
\end{equation}
where $G^0=B^0=1$. Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-majorant-power-vanishing}
 \partial_t^jD_y^k(G^m)(0,0)=0
 \qquad\text{whenever}\qquad j+k<m.
\end{equation}
To verify~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-power-vanishing}, apply the mixed Leibniz rule to the product of the $m$ factors of $G$. Every resulting term distributes the total number $j+k$ of derivatives among these $m$ factors. If $j+k<m$, at least one factor receives no derivative and is therefore evaluated as $G(0,0)=0$.

Fix $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$ and put $r\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} j+k$. Since $G(0,0)=0$ and $G$ is continuous, after restricting the neighborhood of $(0,0)$ we may assume $|G|<1/2$. Thus $(1+G)^{-1}$ and $\log(1+G)$ are well defined and smooth there. Taylor's theorem in one real variable yields smooth functions $\psi_{\exp,r}$, $\psi_{\mathrm{inv},r}$, and $\psi_{\log,r}$ near zero such that
\begin{align*}
 \mathrm e^x-1
 &=\sum_{m=1}^{r}\frac{x^m}{m!}
 +x^{r+1}\psi_{\exp,r}(x),\\
 (1+x)^{-1}
 &=\sum_{m=0}^{r}(-1)^m x^m
 +x^{r+1}\psi_{\mathrm{inv},r}(x),\\
 \log(1+x)
 &=\sum_{m=1}^{r}\frac{(-1)^{m+1}}{m}x^m
 +x^{r+1}\psi_{\log,r}(x).
\end{align*}
Empty sums are understood as zero. By~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-power-vanishing}, every mixed derivative of total order at most $r$ of
\[
 G^{r+1}\psi_{\exp,r}(G),\qquad
 G^{r+1}\psi_{\mathrm{inv},r}(G),\qquad
 G^{r+1}\psi_{\log,r}(G)
\]
vanishes at $(0,0)$. Indeed, in every term produced by the product and chain rules, at most $r$ derivatives are distributed among the $r+1$ explicit factors of $G$, so at least one of those factors remains undifferentiated and vanishes at $(0,0)$.

Using~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-powers}, the triangle inequality, and the preceding finite Taylor expansions, we therefore obtain
\begin{align*}
 \mathfrak c_{j,k}(\mathrm e^G-1)
 &\le
 \sum_{m=1}^{r}\frac1{m!}[t^jv^k]B^m,\\
 \mathfrak c_{j,k}((1+G)^{-1})
 &\le
 \sum_{m=0}^{r}[t^jv^k]B^m,\\
 \mathfrak c_{j,k}(\log(1+G))
 &\le
 \sum_{m=1}^{r}\frac1m[t^jv^k]B^m.
\end{align*}
Because $B_{00}=0$, every monomial occurring in $B^m$ has total degree at least $m$. Hence $[t^jv^k]B^m=0$ whenever $m>j+k=r$. It follows that the finite sums above are exactly the corresponding coefficients of the formal series
\[
 \mathrm e^B-1
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{B^m}{m!},
 \qquad
 (1-B)^{-1}
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{m=0}^{\infty}B^m,
 \qquad
 -\log(1-B)
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\frac{B^m}{m}.
\]
For every fixed coefficient, each series on the right contains only finitely many nonzero contributions. We have therefore proved
\[
 \mathrm e^G-1\preccurlyeq\mathrm e^B-1,
 \qquad
 (1+G)^{-1}\preccurlyeq(1-B)^{-1},
 \qquad
 \log(1+G)\preccurlyeq-\log(1-B).
\]

It remains to prove the composition assertion. To avoid confusing the curve with the vector variable of $G$, write $\eta(t)$ for the map denoted by $y(t)$ in the statement. Thus $\eta:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to\mathbb{R}^d$ is smooth, $\eta(0)=0$, and
\[
 \eta\preccurlyeq Y(t)=\sum_{\ell\ge0}Y_\ell t^\ell,
 \qquad Y_\ell\ge0,
 \qquad Y_0=0.
\]
Define the normalized Taylor coefficients
\[
 \mathcal G_{a,b}
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
 \frac1{a!\,b!}\partial_t^aD_y^bG(0,0),
 \qquad
 \eta_\ell
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
 \frac1{\ell!}\eta^{(\ell)}(0).
\]
Then $\mathcal G_{a,b}$ is an output-valued symmetric $b$-linear map,
\[
 \|\mathcal G_{a,b}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le B_{ab},
 \qquad
 |\eta_\ell|\le Y_\ell,
\]
and $\eta_0=0$.
Fix $n\in\mathbb N_0$ and let
\[
 T_nG(t,y)
 \ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}
 \sum_{\substack{a,b\in\mathbb N_0\\a+b\le n}}
 t^a\mathcal G_{a,b}[y^b]
\]
be the total-degree-$n$ Taylor polynomial of $G$ at $(0,0)$, where $\mathcal G_{a,0}[y^0]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mathcal G_{a,0}$. The multivariate Peano remainder formula gives
\[
 \|G(t,y)-T_nG(t,y)\|
 =o\!\left((|t|+|y|)^n\right)
 \qquad\text{as }(t,y)\to(0,0).
\]
Since $\eta(0)=0$ and $\eta$ is differentiable at zero, $\eta(t)=O(|t|)$. Consequently,
\[
 G(t,\eta(t))-T_nG(t,\eta(t))=o(|t|^n).
\]
Let $\eta^{[n]}(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{\ell=1}^n\eta_\ell t^\ell$. Taylor's theorem gives $\eta(t)-\eta^{[n]}(t)=o(|t|^n)$. For every $b\ge1$, multilinearity yields the telescoping identity
\begin{align*}
 \mathcal G_{a,b}[\eta(t)^b]
 -\mathcal G_{a,b}[\eta^{[n]}(t)^b]
 &=
 \sum_{q=1}^b
 \mathcal G_{a,b}\!\left[
 \eta(t)^{q-1},
 \eta(t)-\eta^{[n]}(t),
 \eta^{[n]}(t)^{b-q}
 \right].
\end{align*}
Both $\eta(t)$ and $\eta^{[n]}(t)$ are $O(|t|)$, so the right-hand side is $o(|t|^{n+b-1})$, and hence is $o(|t|^n)$. Since $T_nG$ contains only finitely many terms,
\[
 G(t,\eta(t))
 -
 T_nG(t,\eta^{[n]}(t))
 =o(|t|^n).
\]
The left-hand side is of class $C^n$ in $t$. Its one-variable Taylor formula therefore shows that its derivatives at zero through order $n$ vanish. Hence the normalized coefficient of order $n$ of the composite is the coefficient obtained by formally substituting $\eta^{[n]}$ into $T_nG$:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-majorant-composition-coefficient}
 \frac1{n!}\frac{\mathrm d^n}{\mathrm d t^n}G(t,\eta(t))\bigg|_{t=0}
 =
 \sum_{\substack{a,b\in\mathbb N_0,\ \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_b\in\mathbb N_+\\
 a+\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_b=n}}
 \mathcal G_{a,b}
 [\eta_{\ell_1},\ldots,\eta_{\ell_b}].
\end{equation}
For $b=0$, the inner tuple is empty, its product is one, and the constraint in~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-composition-coefficient} reduces to $a=n$.

Taking norms in~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-composition-coefficient} gives
\begin{align*}
 \frac1{n!}
 \left\|
 \frac{\mathrm d^n}{\mathrm d t^n}G(t,\eta(t))\bigg|_{t=0}
 \right\|
 &\le
 \sum_{\substack{a,b\in\mathbb N_0,\ \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_b\in\mathbb N_+\\
 a+\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_b=n}}
 \|\mathcal G_{a,b}\|_{\mathrm{op}}
 \prod_{q=1}^b|\eta_{\ell_q}|\\
 &\le
 \sum_{\substack{a,b\in\mathbb N_0,\ \ell_1,\ldots,\ell_b\in\mathbb N_+\\
 a+\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_b=n}}
 B_{ab}\prod_{q=1}^bY_{\ell_q}\\
 &=[t^n]B(t,Y(t)).
\end{align*}
The final equality is the coefficient formula for formal composition. It is well defined because $Y_0=0$: for a fixed $n$, the constraint $a+\ell_1+\cdots+\ell_b=n$ forces $0\le a\le n$ and $0\le b\le n$, so only finitely many terms occur. Since $n$ was arbitrary, $G(t,\eta(t))\preccurlyeq B(t,Y(t))$.
\hfill\\
\noindent
Finally, every coefficient estimate of total degree at most $n$ obtained above uses only derivatives and majorant coefficients of total degree at most $n$. Thus the same arguments prove the corresponding assertions for the truncated relations $\preccurlyeq_n$, without any analyticity assumption or convergence of the Taylor series of $G,H,$ or $\eta$. This completes the proof.

body_md:
Fix $\vartheta\in[0,1]$. Write $x(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} x_0+\rho t\xi$, $b_i(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} b_i^{(\vartheta)}(x(t))$, $w_i(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} w_i^{(\vartheta)}(x(t))$, $\theta_i(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\theta_i(x(t))$, $z_0\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} z_{0,\vartheta}$, and $\pi_i\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\pi_i^{(\vartheta)}$; a subscript $0$ denotes evaluation at $t=0$. For sufficiently small $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $|t|<\varepsilon$,
\[
\begin{gathered}
|x(t)-X_i|\ge\rho(1-|t|)>0,\qquad \theta_i(t)>0,\qquad \sum_i\theta_i(t)=1,\qquad c=\frac{s}{4(s-1)}>0,\\
R(x(t))^{2s}=\sum_i\theta_i(t)|x(t)-X_i|^{2s}\ge\rho^{2s}(1-|t|)^{2s}>0.
\end{gathered}
\]
The geometric definitions and~\eqref{eq:three-normalized-data} give $b_i\in C^\infty((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon);\mathbb{R}^d)$ and $w_i,\theta_i\in C^\infty((-\varepsilon,\varepsilon);\mathbb{R})$. Set $Z_\vartheta(t,z)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_i\theta_i(t)\mathrm e^{-w_i(t)-2cz\cdot b_i(t)}>0$. By~\eqref{eq:three-gibbs-dual},
\[
\lambda_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,z)=\frac{\theta_i(t)\mathrm e^{-w_i(t)-2cz\cdot b_i(t)}}{Z_\vartheta(t,z)},\qquad \pi_i=\lambda_i^{(\vartheta)}(0,z_0)>0,\qquad \sum_i\pi_i=1,\qquad \sum_i\pi_i b_{i0}=z_0.
\]
Define
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-log-gibbs-change}
\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\log\frac{\theta_i(t)}{\theta_{i0}}-(w_i(t)-w_{i0})-2cz_0\cdot(b_i(t)-b_{i0})-2cy\cdot b_i(t).
\end{equation}
Lemmas~\ref{lem:three-normalization} and~\ref{lem:three-primitives} give $|z_0|\le3$, $V_i\ge\max\{1,u_i\}$, and
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_i-b_{i0}&\preccurlyeq u_i(b-b(0)),&w_i-w_{i0}&\preccurlyeq V_i(a-a(0)),\\
\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}&\preccurlyeq T+V_i(a-a(0))+6cu_i(b-b(0))+2cu_ibv\preccurlyeq V_iX(t,v),&\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}(0,0)&=0.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here the product bounds are those of Lemma~\ref{lem:three-majorant-calculus}. Since $T(0)=0$ and $a,b,T$ have nonnegative coefficients, $\alpha,X$ have nonnegative coefficients and $\alpha(0)=X(0,0)=0$. In particular, $[t^jv^k]X^\ell=0$ whenever $\ell>j+k$.

Put $Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_i\pi_i\mathrm e^{\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,y)}$ and $N_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_i\pi_i b_i(t)\mathrm e^{\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,y)}$. Substitution in~\eqref{eq:three-log-gibbs-change} yields
\[
\begin{gathered}
\theta_i(t)\mathrm e^{-w_i(t)-2c(z_0+y)\cdot b_i(t)}=\theta_{i0}\mathrm e^{-w_{i0}-2cz_0\cdot b_{i0}}\mathrm e^{\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,y)},\\
Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)=\frac{Z_\vartheta(t,z_0+y)}{Z_\vartheta(0,z_0)}>0,\qquad \frac{N_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)}{Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)}=\sum_i\lambda_i^{(\vartheta)}(t,z_0+y)b_i(t),\\
Q_{0,\vartheta}(0,0)=1,\qquad N_{0,\vartheta}(0,0)=z_0.
\end{gathered}
\]
By~\eqref{eq:three-moment-bound}, coefficientwise in $(t,v)$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-moment-series}
\begin{aligned}
\sum_i\pi_i(\mathrm e^{V_iX}-1)&=\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{X^\ell}{\ell!}\sum_i\pi_iV_i^\ell\preccurlyeq K_0\sum_{\ell\ge1}(\kappa X)^\ell=Q_*,\\
\sum_i\pi_iV_i(\mathrm e^{V_iX}-1)&=\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{X^\ell}{\ell!}\sum_i\pi_iV_i^{\ell+1}\\
&\preccurlyeq K_0\kappa\sum_{\ell\ge1}(\ell+1)(\kappa X)^\ell=K_0\kappa\bigl((1-\kappa X)^{-2}-1\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus $Q_{0,\vartheta}-1\preccurlyeq Q_*$, and $\sum_i\pi_i u_i\le\sum_i\pi_iV_i\le K_0\kappa$ gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
N_{0,\vartheta}-z_0&=\sum_i\pi_i(b_i-b_{i0})+\sum_i\pi_i b_i(\mathrm e^{\zeta_i^{(\vartheta)}}-1)\\
&\preccurlyeq(b-b(0))\sum_i\pi_i u_i+b\sum_i\pi_i u_i(\mathrm e^{V_iX}-1)\\
&\preccurlyeq K_0\kappa(b-b(0))+K_0\kappa b\bigl((1-\kappa X)^{-2}-1\bigr)=N_*.
\end{aligned}
\]
In particular, $Q_*,N_*$ have nonnegative coefficients and $Q_*(0,0)=N_*(0,0)=0$. By~\eqref{eq:three-analytic-majorants}, $Q_{0,\vartheta}^{-1}\preccurlyeq(1-Q_*)^{-1}$. Therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-gibbs-mean-ratio}
\begin{aligned}
G_\vartheta(t,y)&\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\frac{N_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)}{Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,y)}-z_0=\frac{N_{0,\vartheta}-z_0-z_0(Q_{0,\vartheta}-1)}{1+(Q_{0,\vartheta}-1)},\\
G_\vartheta&\preccurlyeq\frac{N_*+3Q_*}{1-Q_*}=J_*,\qquad G_\vartheta(0,0)=0.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The expansion $J_*=(N_*+3Q_*)\sum_{\ell\ge0}Q_*^\ell$ gives nonnegative coefficients and $J_*(0,0)=0$. Hence, with $R_{jk}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}[t^jv^k]\mathcal R$,
\[
R_{00}=R_{01}=0,\qquad R_{jk}=[t^jv^k]J_*\ge0\quad\bigl((j,k)\notin\{(0,0),(0,1)\}\bigr).
\]

For $h\in\mathbb{R}^d$, differentiation of the Gibbs quotient gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_z\lambda_i^{(\vartheta)}(0,z_0)[h]&=-2c\pi_i(b_{i0}-z_0)\cdot h,\\
J_\vartheta h&=h-\sum_iD_z\lambda_i^{(\vartheta)}(0,z_0)[h]b_{i0}=h+2c\sum_i\pi_i\bigl((b_{i0}-z_0)\cdot h\bigr)b_{i0}\\
&=h+2c\sum_i\pi_i\bigl((b_{i0}-z_0)\cdot h\bigr)(b_{i0}-z_0),\\
|h|^2&\le |h|^2+2c\sum_i\pi_i\bigl((b_{i0}-z_0)\cdot h\bigr)^2=h\cdot J_\vartheta h\le|h|\,|J_\vartheta h|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus $|J_\vartheta h|\ge|h|$, $\ker J_\vartheta=\{0\}$, and $\|J_\vartheta^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le1$. Since $\mathcal K_\vartheta(t,z_0+y)=y-G_\vartheta(t,y)$ and $J_\vartheta=I-D_yG_\vartheta(0,0)$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-linear-cancellation}
\mathcal E_\vartheta(t,y)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\mathcal K_\vartheta(t,z_0+y)-J_\vartheta y=-G_\vartheta(t,y)+D_yG_\vartheta(0,0)y.
\end{equation}
For $j,k\in\mathbb N_0$, put $E_{jk}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\partial_t^jD_y^k\mathcal E_\vartheta(0,0)/(j!k!)$. Then
\[
\begin{gathered}
E_{00}=-G_\vartheta(0,0)=0,\qquad E_{01}=-D_yG_\vartheta(0,0)+D_yG_\vartheta(0,0)=0,\\
E_{jk}=-\frac{\partial_t^jD_y^kG_\vartheta(0,0)}{j!k!}\quad\bigl((j,k)\notin\{(0,0),(0,1)\}\bigr),\\
\|E_{jk}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le R_{jk}\quad(j,k\in\mathbb N_0),\qquad \mathcal E_\vartheta\preccurlyeq\mathcal R.
\end{gathered}
\]
At $\vartheta=0$, \eqref{eq:three-zero-parameter-normalization} gives, for every $(t,z)\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\times\mathbb{R}^d$,
\[
\mathcal K_0(t,z)=z-\sum_i\lambda_i^{(0)}(t,z)\,0=z,\qquad J_0=I,\qquad \|J_0^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}=1.
\]

For $n\ge1$, define the finite index set
\[
\mathcal I_n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\left\{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell):\begin{array}{l}j,k\in\mathbb N_0,\quad (j,k)\notin\{(0,0),(0,1)\},\\ \boldsymbol\ell=(\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_k)\in\mathbb N_+^k,\quad j+\sum_{a=1}^k\ell_a=n\end{array}\right\}.
\]
For $k=0$, the tuple is empty, its sum is $0$, its product is $1$, and $E_{j0}[\,]\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} E_{j0}$. For $(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n$,
\[
j+k\le n,\qquad k\ge1\Longrightarrow 1\le\ell_a\le n-j-k+1\le n-1\quad(1\le a\le k).
\]
Starting with $W_1=R_{10}$, define recursively
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:three-W-recursion}
W_n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n}R_{jk}\prod_{a=1}^kW_{\ell_a}=[t^n]\mathcal R\left(t,\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-1}W_\ell t^\ell\right)\ge0\qquad(n\ge1).
\end{equation}
For $W\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\sum_{n\ge1}W_nt^n$, one has $[t^0]\mathcal R(t,W)=R_{00}=0$ and $[t^n]\mathcal R(t,W)=W_n$ for $n\ge1$, so $W=\mathcal R(t,W)$. If $\widetilde W(0)=0$ and $\widetilde W=\mathcal R(t,\widetilde W)$, then $\widetilde W_1=R_{10}=W_1$ and
\[
\bigl(\widetilde W_\ell=W_\ell\text{ for }1\le\ell<n\bigr)\Longrightarrow\widetilde W_n=\sum_{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n}R_{jk}\prod_{a=1}^k\widetilde W_{\ell_a}=W_n.
\]

Lemma~\ref{lem:three-entropy}, applied to the smooth data $(w_i(t),b_i(t),\theta_i(t))$ and the fixed $c>0$, gives a smooth curve $\eta(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} z_\vartheta(x(t))-z_0$ with $\eta(0)=0$ and $\mathcal K_\vartheta(t,z_0+\eta(t))=0$. Put $\eta_n\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\eta^{(n)}(0)/n!$. The finite Taylor coefficient formula~\eqref{eq:three-majorant-composition-coefficient} and~\eqref{eq:three-linear-cancellation} give, for every $n\ge1$,
\[
J_\vartheta\eta_n+\sum_{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n}E_{jk}[\eta_{\ell_1},\ldots,\eta_{\ell_k}]=0.
\]
At $n=1$, $|\eta_1|=|J_\vartheta^{-1}E_{10}|\le R_{10}=W_1$. If $n\ge2$ and $|\eta_\ell|\le W_\ell$ for $1\le\ell<n$, then
\[
\begin{aligned}
|\eta_n|&\le\|J_\vartheta^{-1}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sum_{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n}\|E_{jk}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\prod_{a=1}^k|\eta_{\ell_a}|\\
&\le\sum_{(j,k,\boldsymbol\ell)\in\mathcal I_n}R_{jk}\prod_{a=1}^kW_{\ell_a}=W_n.
\end{aligned}
\]
Consequently $|\eta^{(n)}(0)|/n!\le W_n$ for every $n\ge1$, and $\eta\preccurlyeq W$ in Definition~\ref{def:three-majorization}.

Abbreviate $\mathfrak h_\vartheta(x(t))$ by $\mathfrak h_\vartheta(t)$. The dual identity~\eqref{eq:three-gibbs-dual} and the partition-function ratio give
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathfrak h_\vartheta(t)-\mathfrak h_\vartheta(0)&=-c\bigl(|z_0+\eta(t)|^2-|z_0|^2\bigr)-\log\frac{Z_\vartheta(t,z_0+\eta(t))}{Z_\vartheta(0,z_0)}\\
&=-c\bigl(2z_0\cdot\eta(t)+|\eta(t)|^2\bigr)-\log Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,\eta(t)).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since $\eta(0)=W(0)=0$, Lemma~\ref{lem:three-majorant-calculus} gives
\[
\begin{gathered}
Q_{0,\vartheta}(t,\eta(t))-1\preccurlyeq Q_*(t,W(t)),\qquad [t^0]Q_*(t,W(t))=0,\\
-c\bigl(2z_0\cdot\eta+|\eta|^2\bigr)\preccurlyeq c(6W+W^2),\\
\mathfrak h_\vartheta(t)-\mathfrak h_\vartheta(0)\preccurlyeq c(6W+W^2)+\sum_{\ell\ge1}\frac{Q_*(t,W(t))^\ell}{\ell}=c(6W+W^2)-\log(1-Q_*(t,W(t))).
\end{gathered}
\]
Finally, put $L(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}}\log(R(x(t))/R(x_0))$. By~\eqref{eq:three-primitive-bounds}, $L(0)=B(0)=0$, $L\preccurlyeq B$, and $\mathrm e^{mL}\preccurlyeq\mathrm e^{mB}$. Since~\eqref{eq:three-normalized-bounds} gives $|\mathfrak h_\vartheta(0)|\le1$, \eqref{eq:three-F-normalized} yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
\frac{F_\vartheta(x(t))-Q(x(t))}{\beta MR(x_0)^m}&=\mathrm e^{mL(t)}\mathfrak h_\vartheta(t)\\
&\preccurlyeq\mathrm e^{mB(t)}\left[1+c(6W(t)+W(t)^2)-\log(1-Q_*(t,W(t)))\right]=\mathcal H(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The data $a,b,B,T,c,K_0,\kappa$ in~\eqref{eq:three-gibbs-majorants} are independent of $\vartheta$; \eqref{eq:three-W-recursion} therefore gives the same $W$ and $\mathcal H$ for every $\vartheta\in[0,1]$.

body_md:
For $x=y$, both sides of~\eqref{eq:smoothness-finite-sites} vanish. Fix $x\ne y$ and put $\gamma(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} x+t(y-x)$ for $t\in[0,1]$. Since $|\gamma(t)-\gamma(u)|=|t-u|\,|y-x|$, the map $\gamma$ is injective. Consequently, there exist $1\le J\le N+1$ and $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_J=1$ such that
\[
\{t_0,\ldots,t_J\}=\{0,1\}\cup\{t\in(0,1):\gamma(t)\in\mathbb X^N\},\qquad \gamma((t_{k-1},t_k))\cap\mathbb X^N=\varnothing\quad(k\in[J]).
\]
For $k\in[J]$ and $t_{k-1}<a<b<t_k$, the map $H\circ\gamma$ is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of $[a,b]$, with $(H\circ\gamma)'(t)=DH(\gamma(t))[y-x]$. The fundamental theorem of calculus and the integral triangle inequality give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:smoothness-subsegment}
\begin{aligned}
H(\gamma(b))-H(\gamma(a))
&=\int_a^b DH(\gamma(t))[y-x]\,\mathrm d t,\\
\|H(\gamma(b))-H(\gamma(a))\|_V
&\le\int_a^b\|DH(\gamma(t))[y-x]\|_V\,\mathrm d t\\
&\le\int_a^b\|DH(\gamma(t))\|_{\mathrm{op}}|y-x|\,\mathrm d t
\le B(b-a)|y-x|.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}

Set $\Delta_k\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} t_k-t_{k-1}>0$. For $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, put $a_{k,\varepsilon}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} t_{k-1}+\varepsilon\Delta_k$ and $b_{k,\varepsilon}\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} t_k-\varepsilon\Delta_k$. Then $t_{k-1}<a_{k,\varepsilon}<b_{k,\varepsilon}<t_k$ and $b_{k,\varepsilon}-a_{k,\varepsilon}=(1-2\varepsilon)\Delta_k$. By continuity of $H\circ\gamma$ on $[0,1]$ and~\eqref{eq:smoothness-subsegment},
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|H(\gamma(t_k))-H(\gamma(t_{k-1}))\|_V
&=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\|H(\gamma(b_{k,\varepsilon}))-H(\gamma(a_{k,\varepsilon}))\|_V\\
&\le\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}B(1-2\varepsilon)\Delta_k|y-x|
=B\Delta_k|y-x|.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|H(y)-H(x)\|_V
&=\left\|\sum_{k=1}^J\bigl(H(\gamma(t_k))-H(\gamma(t_{k-1}))\bigr)\right\|_V\\
&\le\sum_{k=1}^J\|H(\gamma(t_k))-H(\gamma(t_{k-1}))\|_V\\
&\le B|y-x|\sum_{k=1}^J(t_k-t_{k-1})=B|y-x|.
\end{aligned}
\]

body_md:
Write $W=W_{\mathbb D^N}$ and $\mathbb X^N=\{X_1,\ldots,X_N\}$. The convention for $N=1$ gives $W=0$; otherwise, $W$ is a finite maximum with positive denominators. Let $f\in\dot C^{s,1}(\mathbb R^d)$ satisfy the prescribed jets. For $i\ne j$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, Lemma~\ref{lem:three-taylor}, with base point $X_i$ and evaluation point $X_j$, gives $|\partial^\alpha(P_i-P_j)(X_j)|\le [f]_{s,1}|X_i-X_j|^{s+1-|\alpha|}/(s+1-|\alpha|)!$, since each coordinate component of a derivative tensor is bounded by its operator norm. Dividing by $|X_i-X_j|^{s+1-|\alpha|}$ and taking the maximum proves (i), the case $N=1$ being immediate.

Suppose that $W=0$. If $N\ge2$, every derivative of $P_i-P_j$ of order at most $s$ vanishes at $X_j$; the exact Taylor expansion of this polynomial therefore gives $P_i=P_j$. For $N=1$, the assertion is automatic. Conversely, identical polynomials give $W=0$. Since the order-$s$ derivative of a polynomial of degree at most $s$ is constant, $g=P_1$ has seminorm zero. This proves (iii) and also (ii) when $W=0$.

We may henceforth assume that $W>0$, and therefore $N\ge2$. If $s=0$, write $P_i=c_i$ and define $g(x)=\min_i\{c_i+W|x-X_i|\}$. The definition of $W$ gives $c_i+W|X_j-X_i|\ge c_j$, with equality for $i=j$, so $g(X_j)=c_j$. Choosing an index attaining the minimum at $y$ gives $g(x)\le g(y)+W|x-y|$; interchanging $x$ and $y$ proves $[g]_{0,1}\le W$. Thus (ii) holds for $s=0$.

Assume now that $s\ge1$, and put $m=s+1$, $D=2^{46d}$ and $q=2m+46d$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:three-doubling-weights}, there are positive probability weights $\mu_i$ satisfying~\eqref{eq:doubling} with this value of $D$. Define
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicit-whitney-witness}
g(x)=\frac{\sum_i\mu_i|x-X_i|^{-q}P_i(x)}{\sum_i\mu_i|x-X_i|^{-q}}\quad(x\notin\mathbb X^N),\qquad g(X_i)=P_i(X_i).
\end{equation}
The evenness of $q$ implies that $A_i(x)=\mu_i\prod_{k\ne i}|x-X_k|^q$ and $A(x)=\sum_iA_i(x)$ are polynomials. Off the sites, every $A_i$ is positive, while $A(X_j)=\mu_j\prod_{k\ne j}|X_j-X_k|^q>0$. Clearing denominators in~\eqref{eq:explicit-whitney-witness} therefore gives $g=\sum_iA_iP_i/A$ on $\mathbb R^d$, so $g\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^d)$. For each $j$, the numerator of $g-P_j=\sum_{i\ne j}A_i(P_i-P_j)/A$ is divisible by the polynomial $|x-X_j|^q$. Since $q>s$ and $A$ is nonzero at $X_j$, all derivatives of $g-P_j$ through order $s$ vanish there. Hence $J_{X_j}^sg=P_j$.

Fix $x\notin\mathbb X^N$, set $r_i=|x-X_i|$, $\rho=\min_i r_i>0$ and $\theta_i=\mu_i r_i^{-q}/\sum_k\mu_k r_k^{-q}$, and choose a nearest site $a=X_j$. Write $B_{\mathbb X^N}(a,r)=\{X_i:|X_i-a|<r\}$ and $\mu_0=\sum_{X_i\in B_{\mathbb X^N}(a,\rho)}\mu_i$. The ball contains $a$, so $\mu_0>0$, and its sites have distance less than $2\rho$ from $x$. Consequently, $\sum_i\mu_i r_i^{-q}\ge(2\rho)^{-q}\mu_0$. For each $\ell\ge0$, the shell $2^\ell\rho\le r_i<2^{\ell+1}\rho$ lies in $B_{\mathbb X^N}(a,2^{\ell+2}\rho)$ and has mass at most $D^{\ell+2}\mu_0$ by repeated application of~\eqref{eq:doubling}. Since $q>m$ and $D2^{m-q}=2^{-m}\le1/4$, we obtain
\[
\sum_i\mu_i r_i^{m-q}\le D^2\mu_0\rho^{m-q}\sum_{\ell=0}^{\infty}(D2^{m-q})^\ell\le\frac43D^2\mu_0\rho^{m-q}.
\]
Dividing by the preceding lower bound for the denominator gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicit-whitney-distance-moment}
\sum_i\theta_i r_i^m\le\frac43\,2^qD^2\rho^m=\frac43\,4^mD^3\rho^m.
\end{equation}

Let $\xi$ be a unit vector, put $P_a=P_j$ and $h(t)=g(x+\rho t\xi)-P_a(x+\rho t\xi)$, and keep $x,\rho,a$ fixed throughout the following coefficient calculations. For scalar Taylor series $B,C$, write $B\preccurlyeq C$ if $C$ has nonnegative coefficients and $|[t^k]B|\le[t^k]C$ for every $k\ge0$. The triangle inequality and coefficient convolution show that these bounds are preserved under sums and products. Set $a_i=\rho\langle x-X_i,\xi\rangle/r_i^2$ and $b_i=\rho^2/r_i^2$, so $|a_i|\le1$ and $0<b_i\le1$. The normalized kernel $\gamma_i(t)=(|x+\rho t\xi-X_i|/r_i)^{-q}$ equals $(1+2a_it+b_it^2)^{-q/2}$. Thus the binomial expansion gives $\gamma_i\preccurlyeq U$ and $\gamma_i-1\preccurlyeq U-1$, where $U(t)=(1-2t-t^2)^{-q/2}$. For $Z(t)=\sum_i\theta_i\gamma_i(t)$, we have $Z(0)=1$ and $Z-1\preccurlyeq U-1$. Since $Z-1$ has zero constant coefficient, only finitely many powers contribute to each coefficient of its geometric inverse; hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicit-whitney-reciprocal}
Z^{-1}=\sum_{\ell\ge0}(-1)^\ell(Z-1)^\ell\preccurlyeq\sum_{\ell\ge0}(U-1)^\ell=(2-U)^{-1}.
\end{equation}

For $i\ne j$ and $|\alpha|\le s$, the ordered pair $(i,j)$ in the definition of $W$ gives $|\partial^\alpha(P_i-P_a)(a)|\le W|X_i-a|^{m-|\alpha|}\le W(2r_i)^{m-|\alpha|}$, because $|X_i-a|\le r_i+\rho\le2r_i$. The same bound holds for $i=j$, when the polynomial difference is zero. Put $V(t)=\sum_{k=0}^s[\sqrt d(1+t)/2]^k/k!$. Expanding $P_i-P_a$ at $a$, grouping equal degrees by the multinomial formula, and using $\|x-a\|_1\le\sqrt d\,\rho$, $\|\xi\|_1\le\sqrt d$ and $\rho\le r_i$, we obtain
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_i(x+\rho t\xi)-P_a(x+\rho t\xi)&\preccurlyeq W\sum_{k=0}^s\frac{(2r_i)^{m-k}[\sqrt d\,\rho(1+t)]^k}{k!}\\
&\preccurlyeq W(2r_i)^mV(t).
\end{aligned}
\]
The identity $h=Z^{-1}\sum_i\theta_i\gamma_i\bigl(P_i(x+\rho t\xi)-P_a(x+\rho t\xi)\bigr)$ and~\eqref{eq:explicit-whitney-reciprocal} therefore imply
\begin{equation}\label{eq:explicit-whitney-value-majorant}
h(t)\preccurlyeq B_x(t)\ensuremath{\stackrel{\mbox{\upshape\tiny def.}}{=}} W2^m\left(\sum_i\theta_i r_i^m\right)\frac{U(t)V(t)}{2-U(t)}.
\end{equation}

Choose $\delta=(16q)^{-1}$ and set $u=2\delta+\delta^2$. Since $0\le u\le3/(16q)\le3/16<1/2$, the inequality $-\log(1-u)\le2u$ yields $U(\delta)\le\mathrm{e}^{3/16}\le16/13$, where the last inequality follows by comparing the exponential and geometric series. In particular, $U(\delta)/(2-U(\delta))\le8/5<2$. Moreover, $d\ge1$ and $\delta\le1$ give $V(\delta)\le d^{s/2}\sum_{k=0}^s[(1+\delta)/2]^k/k!\le\mathrm{e}\,d^{s/2}$. These estimates ensure convergence of the nonnegative majorant at $\delta$, and~\eqref{eq:explicit-whitney-distance-moment} gives $B_x(\delta)\le(8\mathrm{e}/3)8^mD^3d^{s/2}W\rho^m$. Since $[t^m]B_x\le\delta^{-m}B_x(\delta)$ and $D^mP_a=0$, it follows from~\eqref{eq:explicit-whitney-value-majorant} that
\[
|D^mg(x)[\xi^m]|=m!\rho^{-m}|[t^m]h|\le\frac{8\mathrm{e}}{3}\,8^mD^3d^{s/2}m!(16q)^mW.
\]
The polarization estimate in Lemma~\ref{lem:three-taylor}, applied at order $m$, has factor $m^m/m!$. Therefore, using $\mathrm{e}<3$,
\[
\|D^mg(x)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\frac{8\mathrm{e}}{3}D^3d^{s/2}[128mq]^mW\le8D^3d^{s/2}[128mq]^mW=\kappa_{d,s}W.
\]

By continuity of $D^mg$, this bound also holds at the sites. For arbitrary $x,y\in\mathbb R^d$, the fundamental theorem of calculus gives
\[
D^sg(y)-D^sg(x)=\int_0^1D^{s+1}g(x+t(y-x))[y-x,\,\cdot\,]\,\mathrm dt.
\]
Taking operator norms yields $[g]_{s,1}\le\kappa_{d,s}W$, proving (ii). The estimates are independent of $N$, the individual atomic masses and the separation of the sites: the local mass cancels in~\eqref{eq:explicit-whitney-distance-moment}, and the factor $\rho^m$ cancels upon differentiation.

Finally, put $t=d+s\ge2$. Then $m\le t$, $m\le2s$, $q\le48t$, $d\le t$ and $6144\le t^{13}$. Also, $\log2<7/10$ and $d\ge1$ give $2^{138d+3}\le\mathrm{e}^{100d}$. Consequently,
$
\kappa_{d,s}\le\mathrm{e}^{100d}t^{s/2}[6144t^2]^m\le\mathrm{e}^{100d}t^{s/2+15m}\le\mathrm{e}^{100d}t^{32s},
$ and we are done.

\label{prop:dualization}
                                                                                
In Setting~\ref{TheSetting}, let $s\ge2$, $D=2^{46d}$, and $\mu\in\Delta_{N:D}$. If $G$ denotes the $\vartheta=1$ right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:entropy-variance-extension__primal} and $F$ denotes the right-hand side of~\eqref{eq:entropy-variance-extension}, then, for every $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$,
\[
    G(x)=F(x).
\]
